The '''''United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act'''''{{efn|Full title: '''An Act respecting the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples'''}} ({{langx|fr|Loi sur la Déclaration des Nations Unies sur les droits des peuples autochtones}}, also known as '''UNDA''' or formerly '''Bill C-15''') is a law enacted by the [[Parliament of Canada]] and introduced during the second session of the [[43rd Canadian Parliament]] in 2020.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web|title=LEGISinfo - House Government Bill C-15 (43-2)|url=https://www.parl.ca/LegisInfo/BillDetails.aspx?Language=E&billId=11007812|access-date=2020-12-04|website=www.parl.ca}}</ref> The legislation establishes a legal framework and timeline to bring Canadian law into alignment with the United Nations' [[Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples]] (UNDRIP).<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|title=Liberals introduce bill to implement UN Indigenous rights declaration {{!}} CBC News|language=en-US|work=CBC|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/liberals-introduce-undrip-legislation-1.5826523|access-date=2020-12-04}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Raschkowan |first=Linsey |date=2020-12-03|title=Proposed bill would bring Canadian law in line with UNDRIP|url=https://ipolitics.ca/2020/12/03/proposed-bill-would-bring-canadian-law-in-line-with-undrip/|access-date=2025-09-04|website=iPolitics|language=en-US}}</ref>

The law requires the federal government to ensure Canadian law is consistent with the declaration's 46 articles, working with [[First Nations in Canada|First Nations]], [[Métis]], and [[Inuit]] peoples. A key element is requiring [[free, prior and informed consent]] (FPIC) with the Indigenous peoples.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news|last=Kirkup|first=Kristy|date=2020-12-03|title=Liberals table bill to implement United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples|work=[[The Globe and Mail]]|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-liberals-table-bill-to-implement-united-nations-declaration-on-the/|access-date=2020-12-04}}</ref> It also requires an action plan within two years of its passage to achieve the declaration's objectives, and an annual report on progress made.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Two years later, in 2023, the action plan was published by the [[Government of Canada]].

The legislation is part of the government's response to a recommendation from the [[Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada|Truth and Reconciliation Commission]] (TRC) to adopt and implement UNDRIP as the framework for reconciliation.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> It also responds to the [[Missing and murdered Indigenous women#Canadian National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women|National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls]] (MMIWG).<ref name=":3" />

Then [[Assembly of First Nations]] Chief [[Perry Bellegarde]] noted that, while the bill at the time was not perfect, he welcomed and supported the legislation.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite news|last=Alhmidi|first=Maan|date=2020-12-03|title=Liberals table bill to implement UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples|work=[[Toronto Star]]|url=https://www.thestar.com/politics/2020/12/03/bill-to-enshrine-un-declaration-on-the-rights-of-indigenous-peoples-in-canadian-law.html|access-date=2020-12-04}}</ref>

When introduced as a bill, it had the support of 37 Indigenous Nations and governments and other organizations, and 125 human rights advocates.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|last=Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee)|date=2021-03-10|title=Indigenous Nations, organizations and prominent individuals support federal implementation of UN Indigenous rights Declaration|url=https://www.newswire.ca/news-releases/indigenous-nations-organizations-and-prominent-individuals-support-federal-implementation-of-un-indigenous-rights-declaration-815230003.html|access-date=2021-03-13|website=www.newswire.ca|language=en}}</ref>

== Action Plan ==
On June 21, 2023, exactly two years after the act came into force, the Action Plan was released and available on the Government of Canada's website.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Department of Justice, Canada|date=2023-06-21 |title=An important step in upholding the human rights of Indigenous peoples in Canada |url=https://www.canada.ca/en/department-justice/news/2023/06/an-important-step-in-upholding-the-human-rights-of-indigenous-peoples-in-canada.html |access-date=2024-06-23 |website=[[Government of Canada]]}}</ref>

The draft plan received a "chilly reception" at a meeting of the Assembly of First Nations.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Forester |first=Brett |date=2023-04-05 |title=Justice minister pitches Assembly of First Nations with 'imperfect' UNDRIP plan |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/lametti-afn-undrip-imperfect-1.6802904 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230407011557/https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/lametti-afn-undrip-imperfect-1.6802904 |archive-date=2023-04-07 |access-date=2025-04-28 |work=CBC News}}</ref>

== History ==
===Canada and the declaration===
Canada led efforts to weaken the draft declaration in 2002 and 2003, alongside Australia, New Zealand and the United States, though this was only revealed in 2024.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Forester |first=Brett |date=2024-01-15 |title=Canada led efforts to weaken original UN Indigenous rights declaration |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/canada-australia-un-indigenous-rights-declaration-1.7080734 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240119145615/https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/canada-australia-un-indigenous-rights-declaration-1.7080734 |archive-date=2024-01-19 |access-date=2025-04-27 |work=CBC News}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Hurst |first=Daniel |date=2023-12-31 |title=Howard government worked with Canada to oppose UN declaration on Indigenous rights |url=https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2024/jan/01/howard-government-canada-un-declaration-indigenous-rights |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240119183859/https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2024/jan/01/howard-government-canada-un-declaration-indigenous-rights |archive-date=2024-01-19 |access-date=2025-04-27 |work=The Guardian}}</ref>

The UN resolution was passed in 2007.<ref name=":02">{{Cite news |last1=Galimberti |first1=Simone |last2=Shakya |first2=Prabindra |date=2025-03-18 |title=Indigenous peoples' rights: The ASEAN paradox |url=https://www.thejakartapost.com/opinion/2025/03/18/indigenous-peoples-rights-the-asean-paradox.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250318040626/https://www.thejakartapost.com/opinion/2025/03/18/indigenous-peoples-rights-the-asean-paradox.html |archive-date=2025-03-18 |access-date=2025-04-27 |work=The Jakarta Post}}</ref> Four countries voted against the resolution: Australia, New Zealand and the United States.<ref name=":12">{{Cite news |last=Taonui |first=Rawiri |date=2017-09-13 |title=UNDRIP at 10: Are we making progress in the global fight for Indigenous rights? |url=https://opencanada.org/undrip-10-are-we-making-progress-global-fight-indigenous-rights/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201124041922/https://opencanada.org/undrip-10-are-we-making-progress-global-fight-indigenous-rights/ |archive-date=2020-11-24 |access-date=2025-04-27 |work=Open Canada}}</ref> Twelve countries voted against and 143 countries voted in favour of the resolution.<ref name=":12" />

UNDRIP was passed by the [[United Nations General Assembly|UN General Assembly]] in 2007, with Canada voting against it under a [[40th Canadian Parliament|Conservative government]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Globe editorial: The Liberals are about to pass an UNDRIP bill, and they'd rather not say what it means|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/opinion/editorials/article-the-liberals-are-about-to-pass-an-undrip-bill-and-theyd-rather-not-say/|access-date=2021-06-12}}</ref> In November 2010, the Conservative government publicly reversed its position, asserting its support for the declaration as an "aspirational document".<ref>{{cite news |title=Canada endorses indigenous rights declaration |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/canada-endorses-indigenous-rights-declaration-1.964779 |access-date=8 July 2021}}</ref> In May 2016, [[Minister of Crown–Indigenous Relations|Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister]] [[Carolyn Bennett]] officially removed Canada's objector status to UNDRIP at the United Nations.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Cheadle|first=Bruce|date=2016-05-12|title=Canada now full supporter of UN Declaration on Rights of Indigenous Peoples, Bennett says|work=[[Toronto Star]]|url=https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/2016/05/12/canada-now-full-supporter-of-un-declaration-on-rights-of-indigenous-peoples-bennett-says.html|access-date=2020-12-04}}</ref>

===Roméo Saganash's failed Bill C-262===
Bill C-262 was introduced on April 21, 2016 as a [[private member's bill]] by [[New Democratic Party|NDP]] MP [[Romeo Saganash|Roméo Saganash]] to implement the UN's resolution. Although Prime Minister Trudeau had campaigned in 2015 on the promise to implement the declaration,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brake |first1=Justin |title='Let us rise with more energy': Saganash responds to Senate death of C-262 as Liberals promise, again, to legislate UNDRIP |url=https://www.aptnnews.ca/national-news/let-us-rise-with-more-energy-saganash-responds-to-senate-death-of-c-262-as-liberals-promise-again-to-legislate-undrip/ |access-date=8 July 2021 |publisher=[[APTN National News]] |date=Jun 24, 2019}}</ref> the Liberal government was not initially supportive, publicly declaring its implementation into Canadian law as "unworkable."<ref name="backs bill">{{cite news |last1=Tasker |first1=John Paul |title=Liberal government backs bill that demands full implementation of UN Indigenous rights declaration |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/wilson-raybould-backs-undrip-bill-1.4412037 |access-date=8 July 2021 |publisher=[[CBC News]] |date=Nov 21, 2017}}</ref> In November 2016, however, the government reversed this position, endorsing Bill-262.<ref name="backs bill"/> Nevertheless, Bill C-262 "died on the order paper" in the senate during a Conservative [[filibuster]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Smith|first=Marie-Danielle|date=2019-06-20|title=Dozens of bills, including on sexual assault and UNDRIP, die in Senate amid Conservative filibuster|work=[[The National Post]]|url=https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/dozens-of-bills-including-on-sexual-assault-and-undrip-die-in-senate-amid-conservative-filibuster|access-date=2020-12-04}}</ref> [[Maclean's]] referred to Saganash as the declaration's first "parliamentary champion".<ref name=":32">{{Cite news |last=Taylor-Vaisey |first=Nick |date=2020-12-04 |title=The legacy of Romeo Saganash, UNDRIP's first parliamentary champion |url=https://macleans.ca/politics/the-legacy-of-romeo-saganash-undrips-first-parliamentary-champion/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250427133416/https://macleans.ca/politics/the-legacy-of-romeo-saganash-undrips-first-parliamentary-champion/ |archive-date=2025-04-27 |access-date=2025-04-27 |work=Maclean's}}</ref>

===Bill C-15===
In December 2019, the [[Liberal Party of Canada]]'s [[Speech from the throne|throne speech]] following the [[2019 Canadian federal election|2019 federal election]] promised to implement UNDRIP within a year of its new mandate.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Bell|first=Jim|date=2019-12-06|title=Liberals promise to table UNDRIP law within one year|work=[[Nunatsiaq News]]|url=https://nunatsiaq.com/stories/article/liberals-promise-to-table-undrip-law-within-one-year/|access-date=2020-12-04}}</ref> The tabling of the bill was postponed in early 2020 due to the [[2020 Canadian pipeline and railway protests|rail blockade crisis]].<ref>{{Cite news|title=Liberals postponing planned tabling of UNDRIP bill because of blockade crisis, says Mohawk chief {{!}} CBC News|language=en-US|work=CBC|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/undrip-bill-tabling-postponed-1.5468543|access-date=2020-12-04}}</ref>

On December 3, 2020, Minister of Justice David Lametti introduced the bill to the House of Commons where it passed its first reading.<ref name=":0" /> It used the former Bill C-262 as a starting point, adding new language, provisions, and a purpose clause in collaboration with Assembly of First Nations, [[Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami]] and the [[Métis National Council]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|last=Canada|first=Department of Justice|title=Government of Canada introduces legislation respecting the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples|url=https://www.newswire.ca/news-releases/government-of-canada-introduces-legislation-respecting-the-united-nations-declaration-on-the-rights-of-indigenous-peoples-866026951.html|access-date=2020-12-04|website=www.newswire.ca|language=en}}</ref>

On February 17, 2021 Minister of Justice David Lametti moved that the bill be read the second time at the House of Commons and referred to parliamentary committee.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Debates (Hansard) No. 60 - February 17, 2021 (43-2) - House of Commons of Canada|url=https://www.ourcommons.ca/DocumentViewer/en/43-2/house/sitting-60/hansard#Int-11133850|access-date=2021-03-14|website=www.ourcommons.ca|language=en}}</ref> By April 19, the house voted in favour of a second reading and be referred to committee.

On March 9, 2021 an open letter by the [[Grand Council of the Crees]] (Eeyou Istchee) in support of the bill was published in ''[[The Hill Times]]'', urging its passage into law before parliament's session concludes.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":5" /> The letter's full list of signatories comprises 37 Indigenous Nations, governments, and other organizations, as well as 125 human rights advocates.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite web|date=2021-02-05|title=UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and Bill C-15|url=https://www.cngov.ca/news-issues/current-issues/undrip-and-bill-c-15/|access-date=2021-03-13|website=The Grand Council of the Crees (Eeyou Istchee)|language=en-US}}</ref>

On March 11, 2021 the [[Canadian House of Commons Standing Committee on Indigenous and Northern Affairs|Standing Committee on Indigenous and Northern Affairs]] (INAN) held its first meeting on the bill.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Minutes - INAN (43-2) - No. 22 - House of Commons of Canada|url=https://www.ourcommons.ca/DocumentViewer/en/43-2/INAN/meeting-22/minutes|access-date=2021-03-14|website=www.ourcommons.ca|language=en}}</ref> Witnesses included former NDP MP [[Romeo Saganash]], the author of the bill's predecessor, C-262.

On April 26, 2021 the INAN produced its committee report studying the bill with amendments.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web|title=Committee Report No. 8 - INAN (43-2) - House of Commons of Canada|url=https://www.ourcommons.ca/DocumentViewer/en/43-2/INAN/report-8/|access-date=2021-04-29|website=www.ourcommons.ca|language=en}}</ref> The adjustments included references to [[Institutional racism|systemic racism]], that [[Discovery doctrine|doctrines of discovery]] and ''[[terra nullius]]'' are racist, and shortened the time limit for the action plan from three years to two.<ref name=":8" />

On June 10, 2021 the Standing Senate Committee on Aboriginal Peoples, after the bill passed its first and second readings in the senate, released its report without any amendments but with observations.<ref name=":9" /><ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-06-10|title=Observations to the third report of the Standing Senate Committee on Aboriginal Peoples (Bill C-15)|url=https://sencanada.ca/content/sen/committee/432/APPA/reports/C-15Observationsreport_FINAL_e.pdf|access-date=2021-06-12|website=Senate of Canada}}</ref> The senate passed the bill's third reading on June 16, 2021 without any amendment and received Royal Assent on June 21.<ref name=":9" />

== Provisions ==
The bill is the "first step" in aligning Canadian law with the declaration.<ref name=":42">{{Cite news |last=Bear |first=André |date=2021-05-04 |title=Whether or not you support Bill C-15, Canada passing it would be an important time in our history |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/saskatchewan/opinion-andre-bear-bill-c-15-1.6009060 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250118030745/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/saskatchewan/opinion-andre-bear-bill-c-15-1.6009060 |archive-date=2025-01-18 |access-date=2025-04-27 |work=CBC News}}</ref>

==Reception==

=== Praise ===
The bill was heavily praised by the Cree Nation government, who described it as key to reconciliation.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bell |first=Susan |date=2020-12-15 |title=Implementation of UNDRIP 'long overdue' says key figure who helped draft it |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/cree-undrip-ted-moses-romeo-saganash-treaty-rights-1.5842232 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220122024613/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/cree-undrip-ted-moses-romeo-saganash-treaty-rights-1.5842232 |archive-date=2022-01-22 |access-date=2025-04-27 |work=CBC News}}</ref> The bill was supported by other First Nation governments across Canada.<ref name=":42"/>

The United Nations [[Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples|Special Rapporteur on the rights of Indigenous Peoples]], Pedro Arrojo-Agudo, described the legislation as "a benchmark for international leadership".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Forester |first=Brett |date=2024-04-19 |title=UN expert finds 'flagrant breaches' of First Nations rights to clean water |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/special-rapporteur-un-water-indigenous-1.7179387 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250117071750/https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/special-rapporteur-un-water-indigenous-1.7179387 |archive-date=2025-01-17 |access-date=2025-04-27 |work=CBC News}}</ref>

=== Criticism ===
The bill was significantly criticized by several First Nation governments in Alberta, as well as conservative governments across Canada.<ref name=":42"/>

Although the act requires Free Prior and Informed Consent, it does not explicitly provide a definition.<ref name=":4">{{Cite news|last=Alhmidi|first=Maan|date=2021-02-11|title=Ottawa to define 'prior consent' through dialogue with First Nations: Lametti|work=[[The Abbotsford News]]|url=https://www.abbynews.com/news/ottawa-to-define-prior-consent-through-dialogue-with-first-nations-lametti/|access-date=2021-03-13}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=2021-02-10|title=UN declaration to help First Nations achieve self-determination: Bellegarde|work=[[The Toronto Star]]|url=https://www.thestar.com/politics/2021/02/10/un-declaration-to-help-first-nations-achieve-self-determination-bellegarde.html|access-date=2021-03-13}}</ref> This caused concern from various groups, including politicians and Indigenous leaders. Without a clear definition, some feared it would allow individuals to veto developments that are in the national interest and others feared that without a veto it is not true consent.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=UNDRIP legislation could spell more certainty for resource development|url=https://magazine.cim.org/en/news/2021/undrip-legislation-could-spell-more-certainty-for-resource-development-en/|access-date=2021-03-13|website=magazine.cim.org|language=en-US}}</ref> The bill was criticized by Wendy Lynn Lerat, who taught Indigenous Studies at [[First Nations University of Canada]], in an opinion piece for CBC, describing it as "smoke and mirrors" for decolonisation.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lynn Lerat |first=Wendy |date=2021-05-04 |title=Our colonial history, the colonial agenda and Bill C-15 |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/saskatchewan/opinion-wendy-lynn-lerat-bill-c-15-1.6009178 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210621023540/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/saskatchewan/opinion-wendy-lynn-lerat-bill-c-15-1.6009178 |archive-date=2021-06-21 |access-date=2025-04-27 |work=CBC News}}</ref>

[[Idle No More]], an Indigenous rights organization, along with two other Indigenous groups rejected the bill C-15 outright, asserting it is an attack on Indigenous sovereignty and [[self-determination]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|title=Indigenous Networks and Land Defenders call to Reject Bill C-15 – idlenomore.ca|url=https://idlenomore.ca/indigenous-networks-and-land-defenders-call-to-reject-bill-c-15/|access-date=2021-03-13|language=en-US}}</ref> Russ Diabo, a former advisor to two national chiefs at the Assembly of First Nations, described the bill as, "the Prime Minister [...] attempting his own version of the [[1969 White Paper|White Paper]]".<ref name=":7" /> Diabo criticized the bill's lack of Indigenous consultation, claiming it uses language designed to mislead Indigenous people, and that the, "UN declaration will be interpreted and implemented through the colonial Canadian constitutional framework, instead of respecting international law regarding the rights of Indigenous Peoples".<ref>{{Cite news|last=Diabo|first=Russ|date=2020-12-21|title=Federal UNDRIP Bill C-15 is an attack on Indigenous sovereignty and self-determination: Opinion|work=[[APTN News]]|url=https://www.aptnnews.ca/national-news/undrip-bill-c-15-federal-government-soverignty-russ-diabo/|access-date=2021-03-13}}</ref>

== Further developments ==
The [[Royal Bank of Canada]] was the world's leading "fossil fuel funder" in 2022.<ref name=":62">{{Cite news |last=Woodside |first=John |date=2023-04-13 |title=RBC was the world's top fossil fuel funder in 2022 |url=https://www.nationalobserver.com/2023/04/13/news/rbc-takes-fossil-fuel-funding-crown-2022 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230415133524/https://www.nationalobserver.com/2023/04/13/news/rbc-takes-fossil-fuel-funding-crown-2022 |archive-date=2023-04-15 |access-date=2025-04-27 |work=Canada's National Observer}}</ref> Proposals to set absolute emissions targets for 2030, restrict financing for projects relating to fossil fuel expansion and align with the declaration were rejected by shareholders in 2023.<ref name=":62" />

=== Australia ===
The Joint Standing Committee on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs recommended the federal government implement the declaration.<ref name=":52">{{Cite news |last1=Atkinson |first1=Wayne |last2=Bell |first2=Kevin |date=2024-01-15 |title=Following the Voice failure, Indigenous politicians are calling for the UN's Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples to be implemented. What is it and what would it mean? |url=https://theconversation.com/following-the-voice-failure-indigenous-politicians-are-calling-for-the-uns-declaration-on-the-rights-of-indigenous-peoples-to-be-implemented-what-is-it-and-what-would-it-mean-219695 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240119140003/https://theconversation.com/following-the-voice-failure-indigenous-politicians-are-calling-for-the-uns-declaration-on-the-rights-of-indigenous-peoples-to-be-implemented-what-is-it-and-what-would-it-mean-219695 |archive-date=2024-01-19 |access-date=2025-04-27 |work=The Conversation}}</ref> Senator [[Lidia Thorpe]] introduced a private member's bill with similar provisions to the Canadian UNDRIP Act.<ref name=":52" />
